source.title: Optimizing Deeper Transformers on Small Datasets
source.authors: Peng Xu; Dhruv Kumar; Wei Yang; Wenjie Zi; Keyi Tang; Chenyang Huang; J. Cheung; S. Prince; Yanshuai Cao

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no apparent truncation or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: Reports results on how transformer depth, initialization/optimization, and batch size affect held-out performance on small natural datasets. These are related generalization tests, but the tasks, pretrained encoders, and measurements differ from the claim versions' specified settings.
record.gate_note: The paper's own ablations measure test/dev accuracy under changes to depth, DT-Fixup versus standard optimization, and batch size. The cited prior work on large-batch generalization is not counted as a result. No random-label memorization, interpolation-threshold sweep, convolutional-versus-fully-connected comparison, optimizer-family comparison, dropout ablation, sharpness measure, or memorized-example removal is reported.
record.test_reason: Table 7 tests the batch-size effect on held-out accuracy in a new setting: a RoBERTa-based Text-to-SQL parser on Spider. The shared training configuration specifies 60 epochs; increasing batch size from 16 to 120 reduces development accuracy.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that DT-Fixup enables deeper transformers to train faster and generalize better on small reasoning datasets. They separately interpret the Spider batch-size ablation as evidence that larger batches hurt generalization on small datasets.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses pretrained RoBERTa encodings with newly trained transformer layers and compares DT-Fixup with standard optimization; it does not use the original claim versions' specified image-classification, random-label, or width-sweep setups.
record.method_sensitivity: Spider accuracy varies with batch size (16 versus 120), transformer depth, and optimization scheme; the text also reports that the standard approach fails to train deeper models while DT-Fixup trains them.

fits_no_version.finding: At batch size 16, DT-Fixup achieves 73.24 ± 0.51 accuracy versus 69.60 ± 0.40 with standard optimization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initialization and optimization recipe changes can improve held-out accuracy in small-data transformer semantic parsing.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The batch-size generalization comparison is reported only for Spider and a particular DT-Fixup setup; the paper itself says larger batches narrow the gap with standard training. The batch-size result is an average over five runs, with standard deviations reported.
record.rows_left_out: No additional qualifying results were left out. The paper's other depth and optimization comparisons concern training performance/generalization on different downstream NLP tasks and do not directly test the claim versions' mapped settings; cited prior-work results are excluded.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label versus random-label held-out performance.
Width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD, tuning scope, decoupled weight decay, and optimizer switching.

Image classification and language-modeling workloads; the workload-dependent batch threshold; longer training, learning-rate scaling, warmup, or normalization and regularization changes that recover large-batch performance.
Dropout addition or removal, training-set-size dependence, and excessive-dropout underfitting.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with generalization gaps.
Removing memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the proposed limits_scope verdict: testing one dataset leaves other settings untested, and the narrower advantage over standard optimization does not qualify the batch-size claim. Both DT-Fixup batch-size conditions still outperform the reported standard-optimization baseline. The 60-epoch interpretation follows the shared configuration in Appendix C.5 rather than an explicit budget statement in Table 7.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label fitting or held-out random-label evaluation.
No one-hidden-layer ReLU width sweep or comparison around the width needed for zero training error.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD comparison.
Tests a batch-size increase on Spider under the reported training setup; does not compare language models or broadly vary fixed-epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
No sharpness or other measured generalization-property comparison.
No memorized-example identification, removal, or retraining comparison.

rows.subject: SQL-SP + DT-Fixup
rows.stage_stated: fine-tuned RoBERTa with 24 relation-aware layers trained from scratch
rows.operation_detail: Trained with DT-Fixup at batch size 16 on Spider; accuracy averaged over five runs.
rows.note: The result is a reference point for the batch-size comparison; it does not itself establish a small-batch versus large-batch effect.
rows.check: Valid small-batch reference for R2, but alone cannot establish a batch-size effect. The stage should specify 8 additional relation-aware layers, not 24. The approximately 380-million parameter count describes the main 24-layer configuration and is not separately established for this ablation.

rows.subject: SQL-SP + DT-Fixup
rows.operation_detail: Trained with DT-Fixup at batch size 120 on Spider using gradient accumulation; accuracy averaged over five runs.
rows.note: Accuracy drops as batch size rises from 16 to 120; the authors describe this as an average over five runs.
rows.check: Change partial to observed: accuracy falls by 2.16 percentage points relative to batch size 16, clearly exhibiting the claimed penalty. Table 7 reports five-run means and standard deviations. The common configuration specifies 60 epochs, although Table 7 does not independently restate the budget.

rows.subject: SQL-SP + standard optimization
rows.stage_stated: fine-tuned RoBERTa with 8 extra relation-aware layers
rows.operation_detail: Trained with standard optimization at batch size 16 on Spider; accuracy averaged over five runs.
rows.note: Standard-optimization comparator for DT-Fixup at the same stated batch size and depth.
rows.check: This compares optimization recipes at batch size 16. No corresponding standard-optimization result at batch size 120 is reported, so it cannot establish that recipe's batch-size effect.

relationships.condition: Spider semantic parsing, 8 additional relation-aware layers, DT-Fixup, batch size 16 versus 120 under the shared 60-epoch configuration
relationships.reason: R1–R2 show development accuracy decreasing from 73.24 ± 0.51 to 71.08 ± 0.37 across five runs, extending the batch-size penalty to this downstream NLP setting.
relationships.display_finding: Development accuracy was lower with the larger batch under the shared epoch budget, but this comparison remains unverified.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
